I will keep my land in the usual Quzhou double-cropping system: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That is the system I trust here. Quzhou is a typical North China Plain wheat-maize county, most rainfall comes in summer, and irrigation pressure is much higher in the wheat season, so I would not switch into a riskier cash crop this year. I would use the same plan across all my land and write it here on a `1 mu` basis so it scales directly. For wheat, I would plant an improved local variety, use moderate fertilizer instead of chasing yield with heavy nitrogen, irrigate mainly in the key spring stages, and keep management steady. For summer maize, I would use a hybrid, sow right after wheat harvest, mostly rely on rainfall, keep one irrigation in reserve for emergence or a dry spell, and stay with no-tillage/standing-stubble planting to save time and moisture. I would not push inputs to the highest possible level, because in my place water matters, fertilizer is easy to overdo, and a stable harvest matters more than gambling on a record year. This is broadly consistent with Quzhou and Hebei wheat-maize research and provincial guidance on climate, fertilizer, irrigation, and seasonal management: [PMC Quzhou site description](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5290742/), [Hebei 2026 wheat spring management note](https://nyncj.sjz.gov.cn/columns/86f1c43c-897d-4b4f-b83d-ee6e7fe11683/202602/09/79e5d401-0368-4be7-99f4-7d318cf1d9b1.html), [Hebei summer maize fertilization guidance](https://www.zynylm.com/zhibao/2019/0222/3071.html), [Hebei 2025 maize technical guidance summary](https://www.cfsn.cn/news/detail/616/301792.html), [MOA Huang-Huai-Hai summer maize guidance](https://www.agri.cn/sc/nszd/202206/t20220601_8125506.htm).
